     15	metadata:
     16	  author: nzuresh
     17	  version: "1.0.3"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA, Chat tasks"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, AWS ParallelCluster, Amazon EC2, Amazon FSx for Lustre, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Amazon EKS, AWS Health"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Machine Learning, GenAI, High Performance Computing"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# GPU Cluster Evidence, Readiness, and Fault Verdicts
     24	
     25	For GPU clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or EKS), AWS ParallelCluster, and self-managed
     26	EC2 or EKS. Generic investigation finds the obvious signals; this skill adds what it gets
     27	wrong: silent evidence, wrong-headline hardware verdicts, and predictable failures before a
     28	long run. **Read-only.** Never reboot, replace, update, or delete anything, and never read
     29	training data, checkpoints, or model weights.
     30	
     31	## Critical rules R1 to R10 (apply in every mode, in this order)
     32	
     33	R1. **Answer in one pass, and always leave room to answer.** In chat, do not stop to ask a
     34	   question and do not hand off to a separate investigation before answering. If an input is
     35	   missing, use the default (impact window: last 24 hours; run length: evaluate 24, 48, and
     36	   72 hours), state the assumption, and mark dependent checks `Needs input`. For "slow" or
     37	   performance questions with no time given, use the last 72 hours. Offer follow-ups only
     38	   after the answer.
     39	   **Budget the evidence gathering so the answer always gets written.** An investigation that
     40	   runs out of room before it reports is worth nothing to the operator, and it is worse than a
     41	   partial answer because it looks like a failure rather than a finding. So: collect the
     42	   mandatory evidence for the mode first (R2, R4, R5, and for Mode P the P1 to P6 core), then
     43	   write the report. Pick up the optional checks only with what is left. If you notice you are
     44	   deep into tool calls and have not yet produced an answer, **stop collecting and report what
     45	   you have**, marking everything unreached as `Not checked` with the call that would close
     46	   it. Never end a turn with evidence gathered and no verdict.
     47	R2. **Inventory and capability profile.** HyperPod: `sagemaker.DescribeCluster` and
     48	   `ListClusterNodes` (paginate). Read `NodeProvisioningMode` from `DescribeCluster`: if it is
     49	   `Continuous`, also pull `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` for the window (see rule R11), which
     50	   is the only timeline source that survives broken log delivery. On any other value the call
     51	   is unsupported and must be skipped, not retried.
     52	   EC2/ParallelCluster/EKS: `ec2.DescribeInstances`. For every
     53	   GPU instance type: `ec2.DescribeInstanceTypes` (strip HyperPod `ml.`): GPU count,
     54	   `EfaSupported`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces`; per EC2 node, attached `efa`/`efa-only` interfaces.
     55	   Report `<attached> of <max>`, where attached = interfaces with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     56	   `efa-only` (the primary ENA interface does not count unless it is `efa`). HyperPod nodes
     57	   are not visible to `DescribeInstances`: say so. On NVSwitch types, search every log source
     58	   found under rule R4 for `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` before saying it is not confirmed.
     59	R3. **Node identity survives replacement.** A HyperPod reboot keeps the instance ID; a replace
     60	   gives the node a **new instance ID in the same instance group**, so the current ID will
     61	   never appear in the replace request. Query CloudTrail **by event name, not by instance
     62	   ID**: `cloudtrail.LookupEvents` with `LookupAttributes=[{AttributeKey: EventName,
     63	   AttributeValue: BatchReplaceClusterNodes}]`, then again for `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     64	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `UpdateCluster`, with `StartTime` = window start minus 6
     65	   hours and `EndTime` = now as full ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, paginating with `NextToken`.
     66	   Keep events whose `requestParameters.clusterName` is this cluster. A `nodeIds` entry
     67	   that is not in the current `ListClusterNodes` output was replaced; the instance group
     68	   whose node has a `LaunchTime` just after that event is the replaced group. That operator
     69	   or automatic call is the explanation for the node going `Pending` (Branch E), not hardware.
     70	R4. **Find every log source by substring, not prefix.** Call `logs.DescribeLogGroups` with
     71	   `logGroupNamePattern` (case-sensitive substring) = the cluster name, then again for
     72	   `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`, `journal`, and `gpu`, paginating with `nextToken`. Never
     73	   search only `/aws/parallelcluster` or `/aws/sagemaker` prefixes: customer pipelines use
     74	   other names (for example `/aws/<pipeline>/<cluster>/kernel`). Evaluate every source found.
     75	R5. **Prove coverage before any "no errors".** For each node and source: find the stream that
     76	   carries `kernel:` lines, then bin **that exact stream** by hour across the window padded by
     77	   one hour. **Always name the evidence you used: quote the full log group name and the exact

     32	## 2. NVLink and NVSwitch fabric
     33	
     34	The CloudWatch agent's NVIDIA plugin does **not** collect any NVLink counter (its full
     35	metric list is utilization, temperature, power, memory, PCIe link, encoder, and clocks).
     36	NVLink health reaches AWS only through the system log:
     37	
     38	| Signal | Where | Meaning |
     39	|--------|-------|---------|
     40	| `NVRM: Xid ...: 74` | Kernel log, HyperPod HMA | NVLink error (NVIDIA catalog: immediate action per NVLink workflow, investigatory action contact support). Hardware class |
     41	| `NVRM: Xid ...: 71`, `NVLink: fatal error detected on link <n>` | Kernel log, HyperPod HMA (`reason: XidHardwareFailure`) | Fatal NVLink error; example in the HyperPod HMA documentation. Hardware class |
     42	| `NVRM: Xid ...: 155` / `156` | Kernel log | GPU NVLink flit CRC error / lane error (listed by Amazon ECS GPU auto repair). Hardware class |
     43	| Other `NVRM:` lines that mention NVLink without `Xid` | Kernel log | Driver diagnostics. List them in the timeline with node and hour. **Do not classify** them or call them a cause without corroboration |
     44	| Fabric Manager start: `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` | System log (`/var/log/messages` or journal) | Fabric Manager service started. Applies to NVSwitch instance types (section 4) |
     45	| `CX Bridge device ... is usable for NVLink subnet management` | System log | P6-B200 and P6-B300 only: AWS documents that on these types Fabric Manager configures NVFabric through ConnectX bridge devices, so this line shows the bridge was found |
     46	| Fabric Manager absent, failed, or restarting on an NVSwitch instance | System log | NVLink between GPUs may not be up. Hardware or driver-stack problem: node verdict `REBOOT`, then `REPLACE` if it recurs. AWS documents Fabric Manager as required on P6-B200 and P6-B300; on other NVSwitch types, report a failure as a strong signal but label the NVLink impact `Hypothesis (to validate)` with `nvidia-smi topo -m` as the check |
     47	| `nvidia-fabricmanager.service: ... PIDFile= references a path below legacy directory /var/run/` | System log | systemd path warning. **Benign.** Exclude it before counting Fabric Manager "errors" |
     48	
     49	Sources: [NVIDIA Xid catalog](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/xid-errors/analyzing-xid-catalog.html),
     50	[HyperPod health monitoring](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-eks-resiliency-health-monitoring-agent.html),
     51	[ECS GPU auto repair Xid list](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/managed-instances-gpu-auto-repair.html),
     52	[EC2 public NVIDIA drivers, P6-B200 and P6-B300 considerations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/public-nvidia-driver.html),
     53	[CloudWatch agent NVIDIA metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Agent-NVIDIA-GPU.html).
     54	
     55	On-node confirmation for the operator (not available through AWS APIs): NVLink status and
     56	error counters from `nvidia-smi nvlink` and DCGM, and `systemctl status nvidia-fabricmanager`.
     57	
     58	### On-node NVLink and fabric fields, captured from a live p6-b300.48xlarge
     59	
     60	Taken from a node running driver 595.91.07 and CUDA 13.2 with 8 x `NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC`.
     61	Quote these names as they appear. This is the operator-side evidence behind the NVLink 5
     62	family, Xid 144 to 150, in `references/xid-triage.md` rule 10.
     63	
     64	| Command | Healthy reading observed | How to read it |
     65	|---------|--------------------------|----------------|
     66	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -s` | `Link <n>: 53.125 GB/s` for every link | A link that is missing, or reads `<inactive>`, is down. Compare the link count across all 8 GPUs; an asymmetry is the fault location |
     67	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` | All zero: `Malformed packet Errors`, `Buffer overrun Errors`, `Rx Errors`, `Rx remote Errors`, `Rx General Errors`, `Local link integrity Errors`, `Tx discards`, `Link recovery successful events`, `Link recovery failed events`, `Total link recovery events`, `Effective Errors`, `Symbol Errors` | These are the exact counter names on driver 595.91.07. Non-zero on one link on one GPU points at that link, and these are the counters to quote when an Xid 144 to 150 names a link. `Link recovery failed events` above zero is the strongest of them. Note the older `Replay Errors` / `Recovery Errors` / `CRC Errors` names are **not** present on this driver, so do not look for them |
     68	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e`, FEC fields | `FEC Errors - 0: <large and growing>`, buckets 1 to 15 at or near `0` | **Do not report bucket 0 as an error count.** It is the corrected-codeword counter and reads in the billions on a healthy link (36,140,749,276 observed at boot). Only buckets climbing above 0 indicate real link stress |
     69	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e`, BER fields | `Effective BER: 15e-255`, `Symbol BER: 15e-255` | `15e-255` is the floating-point floor, meaning effectively zero. Do not read it as a large exponent or a high error rate |
     70	| `nvidia-smi nvlink -e`, raw lane fields | `Raw BER Lane 0: 2061`, `Raw BER Lane 1: 1038`, `Raw BER Total: 1037`, `Raw Errors Lane 0: 82`, `Raw Errors Lane 1: 4` | **All of these were non-zero on a healthy node at boot.** They are pre-correction physical-layer counters, so a non-zero value is normal and is not a fault. Never report `Raw Errors` or `Raw BER` as evidence of an NVLink problem on its own. Use them only as a trend against the same link's earlier reading, and lead with the corrected counters above |
     71	| `nvidia-smi -q`, `Fabric` section | `State: Completed`, `Status: Success`, `CliqueId: 0`, plus a per-GPU `GPU Fabric GUID` | `State` other than `Completed` or `Status` other than `Success` means the GPU has not joined the NVLink fabric. This is the single clearest fabric health field, better than parsing Fabric Manager log lines |
     72	| `systemctl is-active nvidia-fabricmanager` | `active` | Anything else on an NVSwitch type is a REBOOT candidate per the table above |
     73	| `nvidia-smi topo -m` | `NV18` between every GPU pair | `NV18` means 18 bonded NVLinks. A pair reading `SYS` or `PHB` instead has lost NVLink and fell back to PCIe or the host interconnect, which is the topology-level version of the SHM fallback in section 1 |
     74	
     75	Two things to watch for, both seen on the healthy node above. The FEC bucket-0 counter and
     76	the `15e-255` BER floor both look alarming at a glance and neither is a fault, so calling
     77	either one an error is simply wrong. Separately, `dmesg` on a healthy node carries
     78	`NVRM: API mismatch` warnings whenever a userspace component lags the kernel module
     79	version; `nvidia-gridd` did exactly that here. Filter those out before you count NVRM
     80	errors, the same way you would drop the Fabric Manager `PIDFile=` warning.

     82	## 3. EFA error counters
     83	
     84	| Source | Metric names |
     85	|--------|--------------|
     86	| CloudWatch agent `efa` section (namespace `CWAgent`) | `efa_retrans_pkts`, `efa_retrans_timeout_events`, `efa_impaired_remote_conn_events`, `efa_unresponsive_remote_events`, `efa_rx_dropped`, `efa_rdma_read_wr_err`, `efa_rdma_write_wr_err` |
     87	| HyperPod observability EFA exporter | `node_amazonefa_*` (for example `node_amazonefa_rx_drops`, `node_amazonefa_rdma_read_wr_err`) |
     88	| On the node | `rdma -p statistic show`, or `/sys/class/infiniband/<device>/ports/<port>/hw_counters/` |
     89	
     90	Read them as signals, not thresholds: a rise in retransmit timeouts, impaired or
     91	unresponsive remote events, or work-request errors on the affected nodes, starting at or
     92	before the hang, supports Branch D. A rise that starts after the hang is an effect.
     93	Sources: [CloudWatch agent EFA metrics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Agent-EFA.html),
     94	[Monitor an EFA](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-working-monitor.html).
     95	
     96	**Counting `/sys/class/infiniband` entries will not tell you whether EFA is attached.** A
     97	`p6-b300.48xlarge` launched with no EFA interface whatsoever still showed two InfiniBand
     98	devices, `ibp198s0f0` and `ibp199s0f0`. Those are ConnectX bridges, driven by `mlx5_ib` and
     99	`mlx5_core` on firmware `28.47.2526`, and they are how Fabric Manager handles NVLink subnet
     100	management on P6-B200 and P6-B300. The AWS public-driver page covers this, and it is the
     101	same hardware behind the `CX Bridge device ... is usable for NVLink subnet management` line
     102	in section 2. None of it is network fabric. On that node the `efa` kernel module was loaded
     103	but sat at a zero reference count, `/dev/infiniband` held only the ConnectX `uverbs` and
     104	`umad` pairs, and `DescribeInstances` showed no interface with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     105	`efa-only`.
     106	
     107	On Blackwell, then, an InfiniBand device count tells you about the NVLink bridge and nothing
     108	about EFA. Reading two devices as two EFA adapters is a false positive waiting to happen.
     109	Count EFA the way rule R2 describes it, from `DescribeInstances` `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     110	`efa-only` measured against `MaximumEfaInterfaces`. If you want to confirm from the node,
     111	`fi_info -p efa` is the honest check, though it is missing from the base Deep Learning AMI
     112	until libfabric is installed. Failing that, look at which driver sits behind each InfiniBand
     113	entry instead of trusting the entry itself.
     114	
     115	## 4. Which instance types have an NVSwitch fabric
     116	
     117	`DescribeInstanceTypes` does not report NVSwitch or NVLink. Use the "GPU Peer to Peer"
     118	column of the [EC2 accelerated computing instance page](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/instance-types/accelerated-computing/),
     119	summarised here as checked:
     120	
     121	| Instance types | GPU peer to peer | Treat as |
     122	|----------------|------------------|----------|
     123	| p4d.24xlarge, p4de.24xlarge | 600 GB/s NVSwitch | NVSwitch |
     124	| p5.48xlarge, p5e.48xlarge, p5en.48xlarge | 900 GB/s NVSwitch | NVSwitch |
     125	| p6-b200.48xlarge, p6-b300.48xlarge, P6e-GB200 UltraServers | 1800 GB/s NVSwitch | NVSwitch (P6e: NVLink domain spans the UltraServer) |
     126	| p5.4xlarge and other single-GPU sizes | N/A | No intra-node GPU communication |
     127	| Multi-GPU g7 and g7e sizes | Yes via PCIe | PCIe peer to peer, no NVSwitch |
     128	| Multi-GPU g4dn, g5, g6, g6e sizes | Not listed | `NVSwitch presence unverified`; do not expect Fabric Manager; the operator checks `nvidia-smi topo -m` |
     129	
     130	For a type not in this table, re-check the instance page. Never infer NVSwitch from the
     131	GPU model name.
     132	
     133	**The number in that table and the number `nvidia-smi` prints are not in the same units.**
     134	On a healthy `p6-b300.48xlarge`, `nvidia-smi topo -m` shows `NV18` between every GPU pair,
     135	meaning 18 bonded NVLinks, and `nvidia-smi nvlink -s` reports `53.125 GB/s` per link. Work
     136	that through and you get 956.25 GB/s in one direction, roughly half the 1800 GB/s listed
     137	above. Nothing is wrong: the published figure counts both directions, while `nvidia-smi`
     138	reports one. Divide one by the other and you will "discover" a half-width fabric on
     139	hardware that is fine. What actually matters is whether the link count and per-link rate
     140	match across the GPUs in the node. An asymmetry between GPUs is worth chasing; a gap
     141	against the published aggregate is not.

Investigative question: Did the GPU workers suffer hardware faults (Xid/NVLink/Fabric Manager — Branch A/D), NCCL transport fallback or EFA problems (Branch D), or did the Slurm fleet fail to launch / get terminated (Branch B/E), during the throughput decline?

Do the following:

DISCOVER log sources by case-sensitive SUBSTRING (logs.describe_log_groups with logGroupNamePattern), NOT by prefix: run it for "distributed-training-triage-b200", then "kernel", "messages", "syslog", "journal", "gpu", "nccl", "parallelcluster", "slurm", "clustermgtd". Paginate fully. List every log group found and which looks like it carries GPU-node system logs, GPU-node NCCL/job output, and head-node Slurm/clustermgtd logs.
2. RECOVER GPU worker instance IDs: enumerate log streams in the GPU-node log groups — stream names typically embed the instance ID or private IP. Report the GPU worker instance IDs and the window during which each has log data.
3. COVERAGE AUDIT (do this before any "no errors found"): for each GPU worker node, find the stream carrying `kernel:` lines, and bin THAT exact stream by hour across the window ±1h. Name the full log group name and exact log stream name for every node. An empty hour = Not observable for that hour. First/last event times are not proof; the last kernel: line is not when logging stopped. If no stream carries kernel lines, say which groups you searched and that none did.
4. SEARCH for faults on the GPU nodes:
   - Xids: filter @message like /NVRM: Xid/ — extract code, instance, PCI bus id, first-occurrence time. Classify each via references/xid-triage.md as hardware / application / sympathetic, and give each GPU node a verdict (REPLACE / REBOOT / LEAVE ALONE / MONITOR / NOT OBSERVABLE) per incident-branches.md Step 4b. (p6-b300 = NVSwitch, so watch for NVLink Xids 74/71/155/156.)
   - NCCL transport: filter for `NCCL INFO` and `NCCL WARN` — determine EFA (`NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa`, `Using network AWS Libfabric`) vs silent TCP fallback (`via NET/Socket/`) vs NVLink P2P (`via P2P/CUMEM`, `NVLS`) vs host SHM (`via SHM/`). If there are NO NCCL lines anywhere, report NCCL transport as Not observable (never infer from instance type).
   - Fabric Manager / NVLink: search for `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` and `CX Bridge device ... is usable for NVLink subnet management` (expected on p6-b300), and any Fabric Manager failures. Exclude the benign systemd `PIDFile=` warning and `NVRM: API mismatch` warnings before counting errors.
   - EFA / RDMA errors in logs.
5. SLURM / ParallelCluster TIMELINE (head node i-01bbde10b04dd4ca8): find slurmctld, clustermgtd, and bootstrap/cloud-init logs.      15	metadata:
     16	  author: nzuresh
     17	  version: "1.0.3"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA, Chat tasks"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, AWS ParallelCluster, Amazon EC2, Amazon FSx for Lustre, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Amazon EKS, AWS Health"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Machine Learning, GenAI, High Performance Computing"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# GPU Cluster Evidence, Readiness, and Fault Verdicts
     24	
     25	For GPU clusters on SageMaker HyperPod (Slurm or EKS), AWS ParallelCluster, and self-managed
     26	EC2 or EKS. Generic investigation finds the obvious signals; this skill adds what it gets
     27	wrong: silent evidence, wrong-headline hardware verdicts, and predictable failures before a
     28	long run. **Read-only.** Never reboot, replace, update, or delete anything, and never read
     29	training data, checkpoints, or model weights.
     30	
     31	## Critical rules R1 to R10 (apply in every mode, in this order)
     32	
     33	R1. **Answer in one pass, and always leave room to answer.** In chat, do not stop to ask a
     34	   question and do not hand off to a separate investigation before answering. If an input is
     35	   missing, use the default (impact window: last 24 hours; run length: evaluate 24, 48, and
     36	   72 hours), state the assumption, and mark dependent checks `Needs input`. For "slow" or
     37	   performance questions with no time given, use the last 72 hours. Offer follow-ups only
     38	   after the answer.
     39	   **Budget the evidence gathering so the answer always gets written.** An investigation that
     40	   runs out of room before it reports is worth nothing to the operator, and it is worse than a
     41	   partial answer because it looks like a failure rather than a finding. So: collect the
     42	   mandatory evidence for the mode first (R2, R4, R5, and for Mode P the P1 to P6 core), then
     43	   write the report. Pick up the optional checks only with what is left. If you notice you are
     44	   deep into tool calls and have not yet produced an answer, **stop collecting and report what
     45	   you have**, marking everything unreached as `Not checked` with the call that would close
     46	   it. Never end a turn with evidence gathered and no verdict.
     47	R2. **Inventory and capability profile.** HyperPod: `sagemaker.DescribeCluster` and
     48	   `ListClusterNodes` (paginate). Read `NodeProvisioningMode` from `DescribeCluster`: if it is
     49	   `Continuous`, also pull `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` for the window (see rule R11), which
     50	   is the only timeline source that survives broken log delivery. On any other value the call
     51	   is unsupported and must be skipped, not retried.
     52	   EC2/ParallelCluster/EKS: `ec2.DescribeInstances`. For every
     53	   GPU instance type: `ec2.DescribeInstanceTypes` (strip HyperPod `ml.`): GPU count,
     54	   `EfaSupported`, `MaximumEfaInterfaces`; per EC2 node, attached `efa`/`efa-only` interfaces.
     55	   Report `<attached> of <max>`, where attached = interfaces with `InterfaceType` `efa` or
     56	   `efa-only` (the primary ENA interface does not count unless it is `efa`). HyperPod nodes
     57	   are not visible to `DescribeInstances`: say so. On NVSwitch types, search every log source
     58	   found under rule R4 for `Started "Nvidia Fabric Manager"` before saying it is not confirmed.
     59	R3. **Node identity survives replacement.** A HyperPod reboot keeps the instance ID; a replace
     60	   gives the node a **new instance ID in the same instance group**, so the current ID will
     61	   never appear in the replace request. Query CloudTrail **by event name, not by instance
     62	   ID**: `cloudtrail.LookupEvents` with `LookupAttributes=[{AttributeKey: EventName,
     63	   AttributeValue: BatchReplaceClusterNodes}]`, then again for `BatchRebootClusterNodes`,
     64	   `BatchDeleteClusterNodes`, and `UpdateCluster`, with `StartTime` = window start minus 6
     65	   hours and `EndTime` = now as full ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, paginating with `NextToken`.
     66	   Keep events whose `requestParameters.clusterName` is this cluster. A `nodeIds` entry
     67	   that is not in the current `ListClusterNodes` output was replaced; the instance group
     68	   whose node has a `LaunchTime` just after that event is the replaced group. That operator
     69	   or automatic call is the explanation for the node going `Pending` (Branch E), not hardware.
     70	R4. **Find every log source by substring, not prefix.** Call `logs.DescribeLogGroups` with
     71	   `logGroupNamePattern` (case-sensitive substring) = the cluster name, then again for
     72	   `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`, `journal`, and `gpu`, paginating with `nextToken`. Never
     73	   search only `/aws/parallelcluster` or `/aws/sagemaker` prefixes: customer pipelines use
     74	   other names (for example `/aws/<pipeline>/<cluster>/kernel`). Evaluate every source found.
     75	R5. **Prove coverage before any "no errors".** For each node and source: find the stream that
     76	   carries `kernel:` lines, then bin **that exact stream** by hour across the window padded by
     77	   one hour. **Always name the evidence you used: quote the full log group name and the exact
     78	   log stream name for every node in the coverage table, and again in the answer text.** A
     79	   coverage claim without the group and stream it rests on is not auditable, so the operator
     80	   cannot re-run it. Any empty hour means `Not observable` for that hour. First and last event times
     81	   are not proof, and the time of the **last `kernel:` line** is not when logging stopped:
     82	   a healthy kernel goes quiet. Liveness comes only from the hourly bins of all lines in
     83	   that stream. A node is `Measured` if one source passes. HyperPod: a missing
     84	   `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<group>/<instance-id>` stream means `No HMA detections`
     85	   when the cluster log group is otherwise live. NCCL transport with no `NCCL INFO` lines
     86	   anywhere is `Not observable`; never infer it from the instance type.
     87	R5a. **Name every resource you looked at, by ID.** A finding the operator cannot re-run is
     88	   not a finding. Whatever you analysed, put its identifier in the answer: the FSx file system
     89	   (`fs-...`) behind any storage claim, the instance IDs (`i-...`) behind any node claim, the
     90	   cluster name, the capacity reservation (`cr-...`) behind any capacity claim, and the log
     91	   group and stream behind any log claim as R5 already requires. "The file system was
     92	   saturated" or "the metrics looked fine" names nothing and cannot be checked. This applies
     93	   to the resource you cleared as much as the one you blamed, since ruling something out is
     94	   only useful if the reader knows what was ruled out.
     95	R6. **Verdict per node, headline to match.** `REPLACE`, `REBOOT`, `LEAVE ALONE`, `MONITOR`, or
     96	   `NOT OBSERVABLE`, against the evidence bar in `references/incident-branches.md` (Step 4b).
     97	   Application-class Xids (for example 13, 31) or HMA `reason: XidUserAppError` with the node
     98	   `Running` is `LEAVE ALONE`. Never headline "hardware error" unless the verdict is `REPLACE`
     99	   or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds.
     100	R7. **Label every cause** `Proven` (measured signal on the affected node, before the failure,
     101	   nothing competing) or `Hypothesis (to validate)` with the one confirming measurement. A
     102	   spike at the same time is correlation. FSx without a saturated metric is not a proven cause.
     103	   Only a `Proven` cause may be called the root cause, in the headline or in a branch table.
     104	   Otherwise write `Leading hypothesis: <cause>`, or `Root cause: Not observable` when the
     105	   deciding evidence is missing (for example a dead control-plane log). Never write "Proven
     106	   mechanism" for something whose trigger or removal path you did not observe.
     107	   Utilization metrics from FSx (`NetworkThroughputUtilization`, `DiskIopsUtilization`, and
     108	   similar) and `GPUPowerUtilization` are already percent from 0 to 100: a value of `0.9` is
     109	   0.9 percent. Quote the raw value with a percent sign.
     110	R8. **Recovery questions** always state three things: whether automatic node recovery is on
     111	   (`NodeRecovery`), what it does (reboot or replace the node), and that the **job** resumes
     112	   only with checkpoints plus the orchestrator's auto-resume (Slurm on HyperPod:
     113	   `srun --auto-resume=1`).
     114	R9. **Capacity Blocks** begin terminating instances 30 minutes before the end time (60 for
     115	   UltraServers); blocks end at 11:30 UTC and termination starts at 11:00 UTC on the last day.
     116	   For a planned run, write out: usable until = end time minus the lead time; run end = start
     117	   plus run length; hours covered = usable until minus start. Give every value as a full UTC
     118	   date and time, and check the latest safe start is not already in the past.
     119	R10. **Rule out the frequent non-GPU causes** in `references/cluster-edge-cases.md` before
     120	   blaming hardware: subnet IP or network interface exhaustion, ParallelCluster bootstrap
     121	   failures and protected mode, EFA nodes in a public subnet, a Capacity Block not yet
     122	   active, and the FSx maintenance window. HyperPod does not export system metrics to
     123	   CloudWatch, so HyperPod GPU activity is `Not observable` there.
     124	R11. **When the logs are dead, ask the control plane.** On a HyperPod cluster with
     125	   `NodeProvisioningMode = Continuous`, `sagemaker.ListClusterEvents` gives you a node and
     126	   cluster timeline that owes nothing to a log agent, so it keeps answering when a stream has
     127	   gone silent or a node has disappeared. Filter the window with `EventTimeAfter` and
     128	   `EventTimeBefore`, narrow with `NodeId` or `InstanceGroupName`, sort with
     129	   `SortBy=EventTime`, and page through `NextToken`. Where a `Description` is not
     130	   self-explanatory, `DescribeClusterEvent` has the detail. Note that the response has no
     131	   severity or level field at all, so any grouping you apply is your own and should be
     132	   described that way. If `NodeProvisioningMode` is anything other than `Continuous` the call
     133	   is not supported; write `ListClusterEvents not supported` in the coverage table and carry
     134	   on. What you must not do is report a dead log as "no events" without either trying this
     135	   source or saying it was unavailable.
     136	
     137	## Pick the mode
     138	
     139	| The user asks | Mode | Steps to run |
     140	|---------------|------|--------------|
     141	| Something failed, hung, slowed, or lost nodes | **I: Incident** | Steps 1 to 7 |
     142	| "Were there GPU errors?", "Can I trust the logs?" | **C: Coverage audit** | Steps 1 to 3, then 6 and 7 |
     143	| "Is the cluster ready for a long run?", Capacity Block ending | **P: Pre-flight** | Steps 1 to 3, then 5P, 6 and 7 |
     144	
     145	## Workflow checklist
     146	
     147	Work through these in order and tick each one as it completes. Skip only the steps the
     148	mode table excludes. Every step below has a matching `## Step N` section with its detail.
     149	
     150	- [ ] Step 1: Scope the request: account, region, cluster or instance IDs, impact window
     151	- [ ] Step 2: Build the inventory, capability profile, and one ordered timeline
     152	- [ ] Step 3: Prove GPU log coverage per node before looking for errors
     153	- [ ] Step 4: Classify each fault and give every node a verdict
     154	- [ ] Step 5: Pull metrics and settle the root-cause branch
     155	- [ ] Step 5P: Score pre-flight checks P1 to P16 (Mode P only, replaces Steps 4 and 5)
     156	- [ ] Step 6: Write the report in the required format
     157	- [ ] Step 7: Self-check the finished output, then present it
     158	
     159	## Step 1: Scope
     160	
     161	Account, region, cluster name or instance IDs, workload, impact window (default last 24 hours,
     162	stated). Classify the symptom to pick a starting branch (Step 5), but collect evidence for all.
     163	
     164	## Step 2: Inventory and timeline
     165	
     166	Load [references/inventory-and-timeline.md](references/inventory-and-timeline.md) for the
     167	inventory API calls and the eight timeline sources, and
     168	[references/cluster-edge-cases.md](references/cluster-edge-cases.md) for the frequent non-GPU
     169	causes to rule out under rule R10:
     170	
     171	```
     172	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/inventory-and-timeline.md")
     173	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/cluster-edge-cases.md")
     174	```
     175	
     176	Build one ordered timeline for the window plus 30 minutes each side: node state, HMA
     177	detections, Xids, AWS Health, EC2 status and scheduled events, Capacity Block and training plan
     178	end times, and CloudTrail cluster changes (rule R3).
     179	
     180	## Step 3: Coverage audit
     181	
     182	Load [references/coverage-audit.md](references/coverage-audit.md) for the log-source discovery
     183	and hourly coverage queries, and
     184	[references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md](references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md) for NCCL transport, NVLink and
     185	NVSwitch, and EFA signals:
     186	
     187	```
     188	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/coverage-audit.md")
     189	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md")
     190	```
     191	
     192	Produce the coverage table and the node capability and fabric table for every affected node.
     193	Every row names the full log group name and the exact log stream name that row's verdict rests
     194	on, so the operator can re-run the same query. Where no stream carries kernel lines, say which
     195	groups you searched and that none did.
     196	
     197	## Step 4: Classify faults and give node verdicts
     198	
     199	Load [references/xid-triage.md](references/xid-triage.md) for the Xid catalog and per-code
     200	verdicts, and [references/incident-branches.md](references/incident-branches.md) for the node
     201	verdict evidence bar and branches A to F:
     202	
     203	```
     204	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/xid-triage.md")
     205	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/incident-branches.md")
     206	```
     207	
     208	## Step 5: Metrics and root-cause branch
     209	
     210	Load [references/signals-and-thresholds.md](references/signals-and-thresholds.md) for metric
     211	names, dimensions, and thresholds:
     212	
     213	```
     214	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/signals-and-thresholds.md")
     215	```
     216	
     217	Pull FSx (correct dimensions per metric), GPU activity (`AWS/EC2` `GPUPowerUtilization`, unit
     218	Percent, or `CWAgent`), and EFA counters, then evaluate branches A (hardware), B (capacity
     219	lifecycle), C (storage), D (NCCL, NVLink/NVSwitch, EFA), E (cluster change), and F (application,
     220	only after A to E are ruled out), as defined in `incident-branches.md`. Recommend operator
     221	actions only.
     222	
     223	## Step 5P: Pre-flight readiness (Mode P)
     224	
     225	Load [references/preflight.md](references/preflight.md) for pre-flight checks P1 to P16:
     226	
     227	```
     228	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/preflight.md")
     229	```
     230	
     231	Score checks P1 to P16. Lead with FAIL, then RISK. In Mode P this step replaces
     232	Steps 4 and 5.
     233	
     234	**Work the core first, then extend.** All sixteen checks together cost more tool calls than
     235	a single answer usually has room for, and a readiness question with no verdict is a failed
     236	answer however much evidence sits behind it (see R1). So run them in two passes.
     237	
     238	The core, which decides whether the run can start at all:
     239	
     240	| Check | Question it settles |
     241	|-------|---------------------|
     242	| P1 | Does the Capacity Block or training plan outlast the run? |
     243	| P2 | Is there an extension, if it does not? |
     244	| P3 | Is there a spare node to replace a failure? |
     245	| P4 | Is `NodeRecovery` on? |
     246	| P5 | Are deep health checks enabled? |
     247	| P6 | Is GPU error logging arriving, so a failure during the run is visible? |
     248	
     249	Write the readiness verdict as soon as those six are scored. P7 to P16 then refine it, and
     250	each one you reach can only add a `RISK`, never change a `FAIL` already found in the core.
     251	Anything you do not reach is reported `Not checked` with the call that would settle it, which
     252	is an honest answer; silence is not. If the core itself is incomplete, say which part and
     253	give the verdict you can support.
     254	
     255	## Step 6: Report
     256	
     257	Load [references/report-format.md](references/report-format.md) for the report template and its rules:
     258	
     259	```
     260	read_skill_resource(skill_id="aiml-gpu-training-cluster-investigation", path="references/report-format.md")
     261	```
     262	
     263	## Step 7: Self-check before presenting
     264	
     265	Before showing the answer to the user, re-read your own draft and verify each of these.
     266	Fix the draft where a check fails; do not present an output that fails one.
     267	
     268	- [ ] Every "no errors found" statement is backed by a node whose coverage you proved in
     269	      Step 3. If coverage was not proven, the wording is `Not observable`, not healthy.
     270	- [ ] Every coverage row names its full log group and exact log stream (rule R5). A coverage
     271	      claim with no named source is not auditable and must be fixed before presenting.
     272	- [ ] Every node verdict still meets the evidence bar that justifies it, re-read from
     273	      [references/incident-branches.md](references/incident-branches.md) Step 4b.
     274	- [ ] The headline matches the verdicts. It does not say "hardware error" unless a verdict
     275	      is `REPLACE` or `REBOOT` on hardware grounds (rule R6).
     276	- [ ] Every cause carries a `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)` label, and anything
     277	      labelled `Proven` has a measured signal on the affected node before the failure
     278	      (rule R7). Nothing unproven is called the root cause.
     279	- [ ] Every percentage came straight from the metric without rescaling (rule R7).
     280	- [ ] Every absent signal is reported as `Not observable` with what to collect, never as
     281	      zero or as healthy.
     282	- [ ] Each recommendation names an operator action, and no mutating API call was made.
     283	- [ ] Every number in the answer can be traced to a call you actually made this run.
     284	- [ ] Every resource you analysed appears by ID (rule R5a): the `fs-...` behind a storage
     285	      claim, the `i-...` behind a node claim, the `cr-...` behind a capacity claim, the
     286	      cluster name, the log group and stream. This holds for resources you cleared, not just
     287	      the one you blamed.
     288	- [ ] **There is an actual answer.** A verdict or root cause is written down, not just
     289	      evidence. If you ran out of room before finishing, the draft still leads with the
     290	      verdict you can support and marks the rest `Not checked` (rule R1).
     291	
     292	State the outcome of this self-check in one line, naming anything you could not verify.
     293	
     294	## Success criteria
     295	
     296	- Coverage table and node capability table for every affected node; no "no errors" without
     297	  proven coverage.
     298	- One verdict per node with a GPU signal; headline consistent with the verdicts.
     299	- Every cause labelled `Proven` or `Hypothesis (to validate)`.
     300	- Replaced nodes matched to the operator or automatic action that replaced them.
     301	- Mode P: P1 to P16 scored.
     302	- No mutating API call was made.

{"id": "c69d96d3-ab37-4dcc-84a9-2a76c0899925", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_SepgZDDKjXFmUW0sPKHevz", "content": [{"text": "     1	# NVIDIA Xid Triage Reference
     2	
     3	Source: [NVIDIA Xid catalog](https://docs.nvidia.com/deploy/xid-errors/analyzing-xid-catalog.html).
     4	Descriptions and action buckets below are taken from that catalog. The "Class" column
     5	is this skill's grouping of NVIDIA's action buckets for root-cause routing. Always
     6	prefer the catalog if it has been updated.
     7	
     8	Xids appear in the kernel log as `NVRM: Xid (PCI:<bus-id>): <code>, ...`. On HyperPod
     9	they are surfaced in the `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent` log stream inside the HMA
     10	detection message. On ParallelCluster they appear in the `system-messages` or `syslog`
     11	stream of `/aws/parallelcluster/<cluster>-<timestamp>`. On self-managed fleets they
     12	appear only in whatever log group the customer ships the system log to. See SKILL.md
     13	Step 3a for discovery and the coverage check.
     14	
     15	An absent Xid is only meaningful when kernel logging for that node is proven live.
     16	`Not observable` and `0 Xids` are different findings.
     17	
     18	## Commonly seen codes
     19	
     20	NVIDIA catalog values (description, immediate action) as checked. Where an AWS page gives
     21	a different first step, the AWS step is listed because it is specific to EC2.
     22	
     23	| Xid | NVIDIA description | NVIDIA immediate action | Verdict for this skill |
     24	|-----|--------------------|-------------------------|------------------------|
     25	| 11 | Invalid or corrupted push buffer stream | RESTART_APP (investigatory: CHECK_APP/CUDA) | Application: LEAVE ALONE (unless paired with a hardware Xid) |
     26	| 13 | Graphics Engine Exception | RESTART_APP | Application: LEAVE ALONE (unless paired with a hardware Xid) |
     27	| 25 | Invalid or illegal push buffer stream | RESTART_APP (investigatory: CHECK_APP/CUDA) | Application: LEAVE ALONE (unless paired with a hardware Xid) |
     28	| 31 | GPU memory page fault | RESTART_APP | Application: LEAVE ALONE (unless paired with a hardware Xid) |
     29	| 32 | Invalid or corrupted push buffer stream | RESTART_APP (investigatory: CHECK_APP/CUDA) | Application: LEAVE ALONE (unless paired with a hardware Xid) |
     30	| 43 | GPU stopped processing | IGNORE | Sympathetic: follow the Xid that preceded it |
     31	| 45 | Preemptive cleanup, due to previous errors | WORKFLOW_XID_45 | Sympathetic: follow the other Xid |
     32	| 46 | GPU stopped processing | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     33	| 48 | Double Bit ECC Error | WORKFLOW_XID_48 (solo: RESET_GPU; with 63 or 64: DRAIN_AND_RESET) | Depends on which memory faulted, see rule 6. Framebuffer/DRAM: REBOOT (AWS: a reboot retires the page or activates remapped rows); REPLACE if 64 or a remap failure follows, or it recurs. SRAM with the threshold flag set: REPLACE |
     34	| 62 | Internal micro-controller halt | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     35	| 63 | GPU memory remapping event | IGNORE | MONITOR alone. After a 48, a remap is pending: REBOOT to activate it |
     36	| 64 | GPU memory remapping failure | RESET_GPU | REPLACE (AWS: remap failure needs stop/start to move to healthy hardware) |
     37	| 74 | NVLINK Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK_ERR | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     38	| 79 | GPU has fallen off the bus | RESTART_BM | REBOOT first (AWS); stop/start (REPLACE) if it persists |
     39	| 92 | High single-bit ECC error rate | IGNORE | MONITOR; watch for 48/64 |
     40	| 94 | Contained memory error | RESTART_APP | LEAVE ALONE (contained); MONITOR |
     41	| 95 | Uncontained memory error | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     42	| 109 | Context Switch Timeout Error | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     43	| 110 | Security Fault Error | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; investigate software |
     44	| 119 | GSP RPC Timeout | RESET_GPU | Driver configuration: AWS says these occur with GSP activated and the fix is to deactivate GSP. A reboot alone does not stop recurrence. Verdict LEAVE ALONE with the GSP action |
     45	| 120 | GSP Error | RESET_GPU | Same as 119 |
     46	| 136 | Link Training Failed | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     47	| 137 | NVLink Privilege Error | IGNORE (investigatory: XID_137_FLOW) | Application, not hardware: LEAVE ALONE. An illegal NVLink peer-to-peer access reported by the remote MMU, usually an application bug. Presents as NVLink but is not an NVLink fault. See rule 9 |
     48	| 140 | ECC Unrecovered Error | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     49	| 143 | GPU Initialization Error | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     50	| 144 | NVLINK: SAW Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     51	| 145 | NVLINK: RLW Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     52	| 146 | NVLINK: TLW Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     53	| 147 | NVLINK: TREX Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     54	| 148 | NVLINK: NVLPW_CTRL Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     55	| 149 | NVLINK: NETIR Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     56	| 150 | NVLINK: MSE Error | WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR | NVLink 5 (Blackwell only), see rule 10 |
     57	| 151 | Key rotation Error | RESTART_VM | REBOOT |
     58	| 154 | GPU Recovery Action Changed | XID_154 (informational, about another Xid) | Use its value, see rule 7 |
     59	| 155 | NVLINK: SW Defined Error | RESET_GPU (investigatory: INVESTIGATE_SW_USER) | Software-defined link event: REBOOT only if links stay down; not a hardware verdict on its own |
     60	| 156 | Resource Retirement Event | RESET_GPU (investigatory: IGNORE) | MONITOR |
     61	| 157 | Resource Retirement Failure | IGNORE (investigatory: CONTACT_SUPPORT) | The GPU could not retire the resource, and the catalog notes no repair is possible for lack of resources. On EC2 the support path is to move off the hardware: REPLACE (stop/start). Note the immediate action is IGNORE, so 157 alone with a healthy job is not an outage, but it does mean the GPU has exhausted its retirement capacity |
     62	| 158 | GPU Fatal Timeout | RESET_GPU | REBOOT; REPLACE if it recurs |
     63	| 171 | Uncorrectable DRAM Error | (none listed, qualifier on Xid 48) | Not a standalone verdict. It tells you the Xid 48 double-bit error was in DRAM (framebuffer): follow the framebuffer path, REBOOT. See rule 6 |
     64	| 172 | Uncorrectable SRAM Error | (none listed, qualifier on Xid 48) | Not a standalone verdict. It tells you the Xid 48 double-bit error was in SRAM: check the SRAM DBE threshold flag, and REPLACE if it is set. See rule 6 |
     65	
     66	Note on conflicting sources: the Amazon ECS GPU auto repair page lists 155 as "GPU NVLink
     67	flit CRC error" and 156 as "GPU NVLink lane error". The NVIDIA catalog describes them as
     68	above. Follow NVIDIA, and say the sources differ if the verdict depends on it.
     69	
     70	Other GPU memory signals that are not Xids ([AWS Xid troubleshooting](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/ec2-linux-troubleshoot-xid-errors)):
     71	
     72	| Signal | Where | Verdict |
     73	|--------|-------|---------|
     74	| `WARNING: infoROM is corrupted at gpu` | Kernel log (does not match `NVRM: Xid`) | REBOOT; stop/start (REPLACE) if it persists |
     75	| `Remapped Rows ... Pending: Yes` | `nvidia-smi -q` on the node | REBOOT (GPU reset required) |
     76	| `Remapping Failure Occurred: Yes` | `nvidia-smi -q` on the node | REPLACE (stop/start) |
     77	| `Pending Page Blacklist: Yes` (older GPUs) | `nvidia-smi -q` on the node | REBOOT |
     78	| `SRAM Threshold Exceeded: Yes` | `nvidia-smi -q -d ECC`, under `Aggregate` | REPLACE. The NVIDIA RMA gate for an SRAM double-bit error, see rule 6 |
     79	| `Unrepairable Memory: Yes` | `nvidia-smi -q -d ECC` | REPLACE. No repair path remains; the same condition Xid 157 reports |
     80	| `Channel Repair Pending: Yes` or `TPC Repair Pending: Yes` | `nvidia-smi -q -d ECC` | REBOOT. A repair is staged but not yet applied |
     81	| `Bank Remap Availability Histogram` shifting from `Max` toward `Low` / `None` | `nvidia-smi -q -d ROW_REMAPPER` | MONITOR, and a pre-failure signal worth reporting. It measures remaining remap capacity per bank (a healthy B300 reads `Max: 5760 bank(s)` with zeros elsewhere). Exhausted capacity is what later surfaces as a remap failure or Xid 157, so a degrading histogram is the early warning |
     82	| Fewer GPUs than the instance type has | Distinct `GpuId` (`AWS/EC2`) or `index` (`CWAgent`) dimension values from `ListMetrics`, compared with `DescribeInstanceTypes` GPU count; on the node, `nvidia-smi --list-gpus` | REPLACE (AWS: stop and start). Missing metrics are Not observable, never a low count |
     83	
     84	## Routing rules
     85	
     86	1. **Order matters.** Sort Xids by time per node. The first non-sympathetic Xid is the
     87	   candidate cause; later 43/45 entries are usually consequences.
     88	2. **Hardware class on one node, job failed after:** branch A. Recommend replacing that
     89	   node (not reboot) if the same hardware-class Xid recurs after a reboot.
     90	3. **Application class on many nodes at once, no hardware class anywhere:** branch F.
     91	   Suspect code, input data, or framework version.
     92	4. **119/120 on multiple nodes after an AMI or driver change:** branch E. Correlate with
     93	   `UpdateClusterSoftware` or `CurrentImageId` changes.
     94	5. **63 alone** is not a root cause. Do not report it as one.
     95	6. **Xid 48 is two different verdicts. Decide which memory faulted before recommending
     96	   anything.** The NVIDIA Xid 48 flow splits on whether the double-bit error was in the
     97	   framebuffer (DRAM) or in SRAM: "If the ECC error is reported for SRAM (excludes
     98	   'framebuffer'), check for SRAM DBE thresholds" and "follow RMA flow if exceeded".
     99	   Route it:
     100	
     101	   | Evidence | Verdict |
     102	   |----------|---------|
     103	   | Xid 171 (`UNCORRECTABLE_DRAM_ERROR`) present, or the 48 message names the framebuffer | DRAM: follow the Xid 63/64 guidance. REBOOT to retire the page or activate the remapped row; REPLACE if 64 or a remap failure follows |
     104	   | Xid 172 (`UNCORRECTABLE_SRAM_ERROR`) present, or the 48 message names an SRAM unit | SRAM: the reboot-retires-a-page logic does not apply. Check the SRAM DBE threshold flag. If set, the NVIDIA flow is RMA, which on EC2 means REPLACE (stop/start) |
     105	   | Neither 171/172 present and the 48 message does not say | `UNVERIFIED` which memory faulted. Report the 48, say the DRAM/SRAM split could not be determined from the log, and name the one check that resolves it (below). Do not default to REBOOT as if it were DRAM |
     106	
     107	   None of these counters are reachable through an AWS API. They live on the node, so ask
     108	   the operator for them and hold the verdict at `Hypothesis (to validate)` until you have
     109	   them. The field names below come from `nvidia-smi -q -d ECC` on a live
     110	   `p6-b300.48xlarge` running driver 595.91.07 with CUDA 13.2. Quote them as they appear:
     111	
     112	   ```
     113	   ECC Errors
     114	       Volatile / Aggregate
     115	           SRAM Correctable
     116	           SRAM Uncorrectable Parity        <- SRAM, two separate counters
     117	           SRAM Uncorrectable SEC-DED       <-
     118	           DRAM Correctable
     119	           DRAM Uncorrectable               <- DRAM
     120	           SRAM Threshold Exceeded : No     <- the RMA gate, Aggregate only
     121	       Aggregate Uncorrectable SRAM Sources
     122	           SRAM L2 / SRAM SM / SRAM Microcontroller / SRAM PCIE / SRAM Other
     123	       Channel Repair Pending  : No
     124	       TPC Repair Pending      : No
     125	       Unrepairable Memory     : No
     126	   ```
     127	
     128	   A few notes on reading that output.
     129	
     130	   `SRAM Threshold Exceeded` is the field the RMA flow actually keys on. It only appears
     131	   under `Aggregate`, so do not go looking for it under `Volatile`. If it says `Yes`, the
     132	   verdict is REPLACE.
     133	
     134	   There are two SRAM uncorrectable counters, `Parity` and `SEC-DED`. Report whichever one
     135	   is non-zero and call it by name. Adding them together loses the distinction.
     136	
     137	   `Aggregate Uncorrectable SRAM Sources` breaks the count down by unit: L2, SM,
     138	   microcontroller, PCIE, other. Without the vendor decode table this is as close as you
     139	   get to knowing which part failed, so quote the non-zero one.
     140	
     141	   Two fields settle a verdict on their own. `Unrepairable Memory: Yes` means the GPU has
     142	   run out of repair options, which is REPLACE; Xid 157 describes the same situation from
     143	   the driver's side. `Channel Repair Pending: Yes` or `TPC Repair Pending: Yes` means a
     144	   repair is queued but not yet applied, which is REBOOT, the same logic as a pending row
     145	   remap.
     146	
     147	   Where BMC access exists, NSM Msg Type `0x3`, Cmd Code `0x7D`, bit 0 carries the same
     148	   information as `SRAM Threshold Exceeded` out of band.
     149	
     150	   One caveat on driver versions. Xid 171 and 172 only appear on newer drivers; the catalog
     151	   pairs them with CUDA 12.7 and R565. On anything older, not seeing them tells you nothing
     152	   about DRAM. The current Deep Learning AMI ships 595.91.07, so a reasonably up-to-date
     153	   fleet will have them.
     154	7. **Xid 154 overrides the table.** Its message states the required action, for example
     155	   `Xid 154 GPU recovery action changed from 0x0 (None) to 0x2 (Node Reboot Required)`.
     156	   Values: `None`, `Drain P2P`, `Drain and Reset`, `GPU Reset Required`, `Node Reboot Required`.
     157	   `GPU Reset Required` or `Node Reboot Required` means REBOOT for the node it names.
     158	8. **Unknown code:** report the raw code and message, mark the classification
     159	   `UNVERIFIED`, and link the NVIDIA catalog. Do not guess.
     160	9. **An Xid with NVLink in the name is not automatically an NVLink fault.** Xid 137
     161	   (`NVLINK_PRIV_ERR`) is an illegal peer-to-peer access that the remote MMU reports, and
     162	   the catalog's immediate action for it is IGNORE, with an application-debug flow for
     163	   investigation. It belongs with 13 and 31, not with 74 or the 144 to 150 family. Calling
     164	   137 a hardware error is the same mistake as calling an Xid 31 one.
     165	10. **Xid 144 to 150 have no single verdict. Do not make one up.** These are Blackwell
     166	    only; the catalog marks them NO for A100 and H100 and YES for B100 and GB200, which
     167	    covers the `p6-b200` and `p6-b300` this skill is aimed at. All seven route to
     168	    `WORKFLOW_NVLINK5_ERR`, and that bucket says `<intrInfo>` and `<errorStatus>`
     169	    "must be decoded and evaluated" against the catalog's "XID 144-150 Decode" table
     170	    before you get a resolution. That table is not reproduced here, so work with what the
     171	    message itself gives you.
     172	
     173	    Quote the Xid line as it appears. The fields come in a fixed order: Xid number, sub
     174	    component, fatal or nonfatal, crosscontain, injected, link, then `intrInfo`,
     175	    `errorStatus` and `errorDebugData` in parentheses. Of those, the sub component, the
     176	    fatal flag and the link number are readable without the decode table, so report all
     177	    three.
     178	
     179	    For the verdict, `fatal` on a link that stays down is a REBOOT candidate, and becomes
     180	    REPLACE if it comes back on the same link after that reboot. A `nonfatal` on its own
     181	    is MONITOR. Either way, mark the precise resolution `UNVERIFIED` because the register
     182	    decode is missing, and link the catalog so the operator can finish the job. A bare
     183	    "NVLink error, replace the node" is never an acceptable output for these codes.
     184	
     185	    Before you call it hardware at all, check Fabric Manager and the `nvidia-smi nvlink`
     186	    state in `references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md`. Several of the counters there read non-zero
     187	    on healthy nodes, so that section matters.
     188	
     189	## HyperPod node conditions
     190	
     191	Observed on a live HyperPod Slurm cluster: an application out-of-bounds GPU write
     192	produced `Xid 31`, HMA logged `reason: XidUserAppError` and a DCGM policy violation
     193	(`ErrNum: 31`) within about 1 second, and the node stayed `Running` with no reboot or
     194	replacement.
     195	
     196	HMA messages include a node condition such as `NvidiaErrorReboot` or
     197	`NvidiaErrorTerminate`, and EventBridge node health events can carry
     198	`HealthStatusReason`, `RepairAction`, and `Recommendation`. Quote these verbatim in the
     199	report. They describe the action HyperPod took or recommends."}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}, {"id": "tooluse_8lI1ZKhdFkXL1NAqnde7f0", "content": [{"text": "     1	# GPU Evidence Coverage Audit
     2	
     3	<!-- Loaded by SKILL.md. Content validated live against HyperPod Slurm, HyperPod EKS, and ParallelCluster clusters. -->
     4	
     5	## Step 3a: Find the kernel log source and prove it covers the nodes
     6	
     7	Xids are only as visible as the customer's log shipping. Locate the source for the
     8	orchestrator, then prove it is actually capturing kernel messages from the affected
     9	nodes before you trust a zero.
     10	
     11	| Orchestrator | Where Xids can appear in CloudWatch Logs |
     12	|--------------|------------------------------------------|
     13	| HyperPod (Slurm or EKS) | HMA detections in `/aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<ClusterName>/<ClusterId>`. The per-node detection stream appears only after the first detection, so it is absent on healthy nodes. HyperPod does not ship the full kernel log. Also check any customer-shipped kernel log group (below). |
     14	| AWS ParallelCluster 3 | `/aws/parallelcluster/<cluster-name>-<timestamp>`, streams `<hostname>.<instance-id>.system-messages` (`/var/log/messages`, Amazon Linux and RHEL) or `<hostname>.<instance-id>.syslog` (`/var/log/syslog`, Ubuntu). Present only when the cluster's CloudWatch logging is on. |
     15	| Self-managed EC2, EKS, or custom pipelines | Whatever group the customer's CloudWatch agent, Fluent Bit, or similar ships `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/syslog`, the journal, or `dmesg` to. There is no fixed name. |
     16	
     17	How to find customer-shipped groups:
     18	
     19	1. `logs.DescribeLogGroups` with `logGroupNamePattern` (a case-sensitive **substring**
     20	   match, so it finds `/aws/<anything>/<cluster-name>/kernel`), paginated with `nextToken`.
     21	   Run it once for the cluster name, then once each for `kernel`, `messages`, `syslog`,
     22	   `system`, `dmesg`, `journal`, and `gpu`. Do **not** rely on `logGroupNamePrefix` alone:
     23	   customer pipelines rarely use the `/aws/parallelcluster` or `/aws/sagemaker` prefix.
     24	   If the account has few log groups, list them all instead.
     25	2. For each candidate, `logs.DescribeLogStreams` ordered by `LastEventTime`. Keep the
     26	   group if stream names contain the affected **instance IDs** or their private DNS
     27	   hostnames. ParallelCluster and most agents put one or the other in the stream name.
     28	3. Evaluate **every** candidate source before deciding, not just the first one found. A
     29	   node is `Measured` if any one source passes both coverage checks below.
     30	4. If nothing matches, report kernel logs as `Not observable` and name where the operator
     31	   should look. Do not assume there are none.
     32	
     33	**Coverage proof, required before reporting "no Xids":** a healthy kernel is quiet, so
     34	"no kernel lines in the window" does **not** mean the log isn't shipped, and "some
     35	kernel lines" does **not** mean it is. Prove two things per affected instance and per
     36	source.
     37	
     38	**(b) first: find the stream that carries kernel messages from this node.** Run over
     39	the node's lifetime (since launch), not only the window:
     40	
     41	```
     42	filter @logStream like /<instance-id>/ and @message like /kernel:/
     43	| stats count(*) as kernelLines, max(@timestamp) as lastKernelLine by @logStream
     44	```
     45	
     46	(`kernel:` is the syslog-format marker in `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/syslog`, and
     47	syslog-format journal forwarding. If the source ships the journal as JSON, filter on
     48	its kernel transport field instead.) The `@logStream` values returned are the only
     49	streams that can prove kernel coverage. `NVRM` lines among them (for example the
     50	driver load banner at boot) additionally prove the NVIDIA driver's output reaches
     51	this source. No rows means this source does not carry kernel messages for the node.
     52	
     53	**(a) then: prove that exact stream was continuously live through the impact window.**
     54	Filter on the exact stream name from (b), never on the instance ID alone. On
     55	ParallelCluster the instance ID matches every stream for the node (`slurmd`,
     56	`cloud-init`, `computemgtd`, and others), which makes a dead kernel stream look live.
     57	Bin the padded window (start minus 1 hour, end plus 1 hour) by hour:
     58	
     59	```
     60	filter @logStream = "<exact stream name from (b)>"
     61	| stats count(*) as lines by bin(1h) as hour
     62	| sort hour asc
     63	```
     64	
     65	Live means every hour in the padded window has `lines > 0`. A syslog stream on a
     66	running host normally carries systemd and agent lines every hour, so an empty hour is
     67	a delivery gap. First and last event times alone are **not** proof: a stream can have
     68	events at both ends and nothing in between. List every empty hour in the report.
     69	
     70	**Other GPU-communication signals.** In the same pass, record per node whether each of
     71	these is observable, using `references/nccl-nvlink-efa.md`: NCCL transport lines, Fabric
     72	Manager start lines (NVSwitch instances), `efa_*` or `node_amazonefa_*` counters, and GPU
     73	activity (`GPUPowerUtilization` or `CWAgent`). Each goes in the coverage table as
     74	`Observable`, `Not observable`, or `Not applicable`. A missing signal is a gap to report,
     75	never a clean result.
     76	
     77	**HyperPod is different.** HyperPod does not ship the node's system log. The
     78	health-monitoring agent watches it on the node and writes only **detections**, and the
     79	CloudWatch stream for a node is created only when the first detection is written. A
     80	healthy GPU node therefore has **no** `SagemakerHealthMonitoringAgent/<group>/<instance-id>`
     81	stream. Treat
     82	that as `No HMA detections`, not `Not observable`, provided that:
     83	
     84	- the node is a GPU or Trainium instance (HMA runs on these by default), and
     85	- the cluster log group is receiving other streams, such as `ClusterMetrics/slurm` or
     86	  `LifecycleConfig/...`, so log delivery from the cluster is working.
     87	
     88	If the log group has no streams at all, report HMA status as `Not observable` and ask
     89	the operator to confirm on the node that `sagemaker-health-monitoring-agent.service`
     90	is running. Queries (a) and (b) above do not apply to HMA streams.
     91	
     92	Interpret the results as follows:
